Name: refusal_commitment_dynamics
Title: When Does an LLM Decide to Comply? Tracking Refusal Commitment Trajectories to Detect and Repair Jailbreaks Mid-Generation
Short Hypothesis: Refusal is not a single static decision made at the prompt's last token, but a latent commitment that evolves token-by-token during generation. Jailbreaks succeed by causing a delayed 'commitment collapse' where the internal refusal signal decays as generation proceeds. Tracking the refusal-direction projection as a time series across generated tokens reveals a characteristic collapse signature that (a) predicts jailbreak success earlier and more robustly than prompt-level probes, and (b) enables a minimal, targeted mid-generation re-steering intervention applied only at the collapse point.
Related Work: Arditi et al. and Wang et al. (2025) localize refusal to a single (cross-lingual) direction extracted at the prompt's final token. Pan et al. (ICML 2025) and Zhang & Sun (DBDI, AAAI 2025) decompose refusal into harm-detection vs refusal-execution sub-directions, but all treat these as static, prompt-position quantities. Steering methods (AlphaSteer, AdaSteer, SafeSteer) apply a fixed or input-conditioned vector, again decided pre-generation. Deng et al. (2026) note a continuation-vs-refusal competition via attention heads for one specific suffix-relocation attack. No prior work models the *full autoregressive trajectory* of the refusal signal across generated tokens, characterizes the dynamics of commitment collapse under diverse jailbreaks, or uses collapse-point detection to trigger a minimal one-shot repair. We reframe refusal from a boundary/direction to a dynamical system with a decision-collapse event.
Abstract: Mechanistic work has localized LLM refusal to low-dimensional activation directions read at the prompt's final token, and defenses steer along these directions before generation begins. We argue this static view misses a key phenomenon: refusal is a commitment that unfolds over the course of autoregressive generation and can *collapse mid-stream*. We track the projection of each generated token's residual stream onto the refusal direction, producing a per-token 'refusal commitment trajectory.' Across open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B) and a battery of jailbreaks (GCG suffixes, roleplay/DAN, low-resource translation, prefix-injection, continuation-triggering), we find that successful jailbreaks exhibit a characteristic *delayed collapse*: the refusal signal starts elevated but decays over the first several generated tokens before the model commits to a harmful continuation, whereas genuine refusals show monotonically rising commitment and benign prompts stay low. This temporal signature enables (i) an early-warning monitor that predicts jailbreak outcomes from the first k generated tokens with higher AUROC and lower latency than prompt-level probes and Llama-Guard, and (ii) a minimal one-shot repair that detects the collapse point and re-injects the refusal direction only at that token, halting the jailbreak with far smaller utility cost than always-on steering. We ablate collapse dynamics against harm-detection vs refusal-execution sub-directions to interpret *what* collapses. Our work recasts LLM safety from a static decision boundary to the dynamics of an unfolding commitment, offering a cheaper, more robust, and more interpretable defense.
Experiments: 1) Trajectory extraction: extract the refusal direction via difference-in-means on harmful vs benign prompts at the standard prompt position; then, during greedy generation of the first 20-30 tokens, project each generated token's residual activation (best layer) onto this direction to form a commitment trajectory. Also decompose onto harm-detection vs refusal-execution sub-directions following DBDI/Pan et al. 2) Dynamics characterization: on HarmBench/AdvBench/StrongREJECT with 5 jailbreak families (GCG, roleplay/DAN, translation, prefix-injection, continuation-relocation) plus benign (Alpaca) and borderline (XSTest, OR-Bench) sets, cluster/visualize trajectories. Test hypothesis: successful jailbreaks show elevated-then-decaying (collapse) trajectories; refusals show rising trajectories; benign stays low. Quantify with slope, area-under-trajectory, and collapse-point statistics. 3) Early-warning monitor: train a lightweight classifier (logistic regression / small GRU) on the first k=1..8 generated-token projections to predict eventual jailbreak success. Compare AUROC and decision latency vs (a) prompt-last-token refusal probe, (b) Llama-Guard on the completed output, (c) perplexity input filter. 4) Collapse-point localization + minimal repair: detect the token where projection crosses a collapse threshold; at that single position (and subsequent), re-add alpha * refusal_direction. Compare attack success rate reduction and utility cost (MMLU, MT-Bench, over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench) against always-on steering (AlphaSteer/AdaSteer-style) and no defense. 5) Cross-model / cross-attack generalization: test whether trajectory signatures and monitors transfer across the three model families and to held-out jailbreak types. Metrics: AUROC, TPR@1%FPR, detection latency (tokens), ASR reduction, MMLU/MT-Bench delta, over-refusal rate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The collapse signature may be attack-specific rather than universal; we mitigate by testing 5 diverse jailbreak families and reporting per-family generalization. 2) Some attacks may commit to harmful output immediately (no delayed collapse), limiting early-warning benefit—this null case is itself informative and we report it. 3) The refusal direction extracted from prompt-position may not be the right basis for generated-token projections; we validate by also fitting a direction on generated-token activations and comparing. 4) Mid-generation re-steering could introduce incoherence or partial harmful text before the collapse point is detected; we measure leaked-token counts and text quality. 5) Results are on mid-size open-weight models and greedy decoding; sampling and frontier-model transfer are untested, though the dynamical framing is model-agnostic.
